Random masked reconstruction and terminal next-item ranking have a real objective mismatch, already acknowledged by the original BERT4Rec paper. Its remedy includes training examples with only the final item masked; inference appends a reserved mask and scores its representation. Terminal-mask training therefore preserves BERT4Rec rather than requiring a causal backbone. [BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.06690)

Recency sampling provides supporting motivation, but limited direct evidence for BERT4Rec. Petrov and Macdonald argue that arbitrary item reconstruction is weakly aligned with next-item recommendation and expensive to learn. Their exponential sampling favors recent targets and improves several sequential architectures under limited training time; they explicitly did **not** apply it to BERT4Rec. A newer direction, Q-BERT4Rec (December 2025; revised March 2026), uses span, tail, and multi-region masking, but combines these with multimodal semantic machinery, so its results cannot isolate terminal masking’s contribution. [Recency Sampling](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643), [Q-BERT4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02474)

Practical hypothesis for this benchmark: compare random masking against terminal-heavy training within the same bidirectional model, optionally retaining a smaller auxiliary random-mask loss. Sample training-only prefixes, hide each prefix’s final target, and exclude all subsequent interactions from that example; merely weighting an interior mask toward recent positions still leaves future context available. Recency-biased prefix endpoints and a later terminal-only phase are reasonable experimental adaptations, not established improvements on these four datasets. Keep every supervised target hidden, use appended-mask inference, and read the final nonpadding mask position.
